The Tetrarchy was a practical response to the Crisis of the Third Century.
It improved administration, strengthened frontier defense, and attempted to create a more orderly succession system.
However, it was not a lasting solution.
It depended heavily on Diocletian’s personal authority and created multiple centers of power.
After Diocletian’s abdication, rival claims and military competition led to renewed civil wars.
Therefore, the Tetrarchy was effective as a short-term reform but failed as a permanent system of succession.

Launched the Great Persecution of Christians in AD 303.
In AD 303, Diocletian launched the Great Persecution against Christians.
It was the last and most severe official persecution of Christians in the Roman Empire.
Christians were ordered to sacrifice to Roman gods and the emperor.
Churches were destroyed, Christian scriptures were burned, and some Christians were imprisoned, tortured, or executed.
The persecution aimed to restore traditional Roman religion and imperial unity.
Nero blamed Christians after a disaster; Diocletian systematically persecuted them to restore traditional Roman religious unity.
Diocletian transformed the Roman Empire from the early imperial Principate into the more centralized, bureaucratic, and autocratic Later Roman Empire.
